Concrete Driveway Replacement in Dunwoody, GA

Is your home's driveway covered in unsightly cracks, sunken slabs, or crumbling surfaces? An aged, failing driveway not only detracts from your property's curb appeal but also poses severe trip hazards and risks vehicle tire damage. At Brook Concrete Company, we specialize in comprehensive concrete driveway replacement throughout Dunwoody, GA, and surrounding north metro Atlanta communities. We handle every phase of the replacement process—from complete demolition and environmentally responsible debris hauling to subgrade soil stabilization, laser-leveled formwork, and precision pouring.

If you are exploring your options, start by reviewing our comprehensive concrete driveways overview. Our goal is to provide you with a brand-new driveway built to endure decades of heavy vehicle use and regional weather extremes without settling or premature failure.

Recognizing the Signs That Your Driveway Needs Full Replacement

While minor cosmetic blemishes can often be patched, certain structural defects indicate that your existing driveway has reached the end of its useful lifespan. Key signs that call for complete replacement include:

  • Alligator or Web Cracking: Interconnected, spiderweb-like fractures across multiple slabs indicate that the underlying soil has settled or washed out.
  • Severe Sunken or Heaved Slabs: Sections that have shifted several inches out of alignment create dangerous trip hazards and cause water to pool toward your garage or foundation.
  • Deep Surface Spalling and Delamination: Flaking, pitted concrete where aggregate stones are completely exposed cannot be permanently repaired with surface patches.
  • Recurring Drainage and Ponding Issues: Standing water that remains on your driveway hours after rainfall accelerates sub-base erosion and degrades the slab.
  • Driveway Age Exceeding 25–30 Years: Concrete naturally degrades over time due to repeated thermal expansion, water penetration, and vehicle loading.

Our Demolition and Base Rebuilding Process

The secret to an enduring driveway replacement lies in what happens after the old slab is broken up. Many cut-rate contractors simply pour new concrete over old, degraded gravel. At Brook Concrete Company, our crew utilizes specialized hydraulic breakers and mini-excavators to cleanly remove your failed driveway. We haul the old concrete to certified recycling facilities where it is crushed into reusable aggregate.

Once the subgrade is exposed, we evaluate Georgia's native red clay soil. We excavate soft, organic soil pockets and install a heavy layer of crushed granite GAB (Graded Aggregate Base). We use mechanical plate compactors to consolidate this stone base into a solid foundation that prevents future shifting, washouts, and settling.

Replacement vs. Resurfacing: Choosing the Right Solution

Property owners frequently ask whether resurfacing is an alternative to full demolition. If your driveway is structurally intact with sound soil support and only minor cosmetic weathering, concrete resurfacing can be a viable, budget-conscious choice. Key Factors That Dictate Concrete Driveway Pricing

The total investment for a concrete driveway involves much more than simply multiplying square footage by a flat material rate. Professional contractors must evaluate numerous critical variables:

  • Driveway Dimensions and Thickness: Total surface area determines concrete volume. Standard residential driveways are poured 4 inches thick. However, if you park heavy commercial work vans, large SUVs, or RVs, increasing the slab thickness to 5 or 6 inches increases material costs but provides vital structural protection against cracking.
  • Subgrade Demolition and Haul-Away: If you are replacing an existing failing slab rather than building on new ground, demolition costs must be factored in. Complete concrete driveway replacement involves heavy hydraulic machinery, labor, hauling, and local landfill recycling fees.
  • Sub-Base Excavation and Stone Compaction: Georgia's native red clay requires an aggregate base to prevent settlement. Installing and mechanically compacting a 4-to-6-inch layer of crushed granite aggregate (GAB) adds upfront expense but protects against premature failure.
  • Internal Reinforcement: Plain concrete has high compressive strength but relatively low tensile strength. Incorporating grid-tied steel rebar or welded wire mesh elevated on chairs increases longevity and prevents slabs from separating if hairline shrinkage occurs.
  • Surface Finish and Decorative Upgrades: A standard non-slip broom finish is the most cost-effective option. Upgrading to integral color pigments, smooth troweled picture-frame borders, or full decorative stamped concrete involves specialized stamping mats, antique release agents, and multiple protective seal coats, which increase labor and material costs.
  • Site Grading, Slope, and Drainage: Sloped Dunwoody lots require careful grading to prevent water from rushing into garages. Installing catch basins, French drains, or trench grates impacts project pricing.

Why Cheap Estimates Often Cost More in the Long Run

Common shortcuts include pouring concrete directly over uncompacted soil, skipping crushed stone bases, reducing slab thickness to 3 inches, omitting steel reinforcement, and watering down the concrete mix to make it easier to rake. While these shortcuts lower the initial price, they inevitably lead to severe alligator cracking, sunken panels, and complete driveway failure within two to three years. Concrete Driveway Replacement vs. Repair: Which Is Right for You?

When your residential concrete driveway begins to show signs of aging, wear, and structural distress, homeowners face a critical decision: should you invest in targeted repairs, or is it time for complete replacement? Making the right choice requires understanding the underlying cause of the damage, evaluating long-term financial value, and recognizing whether surface blemishes reflect isolated cosmetic issues or deep subgrade failure. In this comprehensive guide, Brook Concrete Company explains how to diagnose driveway damage so you can make the smartest, most cost-effective decision for your Dunwoody home.

For minor issues, our targeted concrete repair services provide an economical remedy. However, when the foundation beneath your driveway has deteriorated, full concrete driveway replacement is the only permanent solution. Let us examine how to evaluate your driveway's condition.

When Targeted Concrete Repair Is the Smart Choice

Targeted repairs are ideal when damage is localized, minor, and the underlying aggregate sub-base remains solid and stable. You should consider repair when:

  • Cracks Are Less Than 1/4 Inch Wide: Thin, hairline cracks that do not exhibit vertical displacement (where one side is higher than the other) can be cleaned and filled with commercial-grade polyurethane or polyurea joint sealants.
  • Damage Is Confined to a Small Area: If 90% of your driveway is in excellent condition and only a single corner or isolated edge is chipped, localized patching makes sound economic sense.
  • Control Joint Deterioration: Chipping along saw-cut expansion joints can often be rebuilt using polymer-modified repair mortars without disturbing the surrounding slabs.
  • Minor Surface Staining: Oil spots, tire marks, or mild efflorescence can typically be removed through professional pressure washing, chemical degreasers, or light decorative staining.

When Complete Driveway Replacement Is Necessary

Attempting to patch a severely compromised driveway is a waste of money. If underlying soils have settled or washed away, surface patches will crack and fail within months. Replacement is the only viable option when:

  • Widespread Spiderweb or Alligator Cracking: Extensive, interconnected fractures spanning multiple slabs indicate deep structural subgrade collapse that cannot be patched.
  • Sunken, Heaved, or Uneven Panels: Slabs that have settled several inches create severe trip hazards and vehicle undercarriage scrapes, pointing to subgrade washout or massive tree root displacement.
  • Severe Surface Spalling and Delamination: When the top layer of concrete has completely flaked away, exposing rough coarse aggregate across wide sections, the concrete matrix itself has lost integrity.
  • Water Pooling Toward the Home: If settlement has reversed the driveway's original pitch, causing stormwater to flow into your garage or foundation, complete regrading and replacement is mandatory.
  • Driveway Age Over 30 Years: Concrete naturally reaches the end of its design lifespan after three decades of heavy vehicle loading and seasonal thermal cycling.

The Middle Ground: When Is Concrete Resurfacing Viable?

Homeowners often ask about a middle-tier solution: concrete resurfacing. Resurfacing involves applying a polymer-modified cement overlay over an existing slab to create a pristine, brand-new appearance. Resurfacing is an excellent option if your concrete is structurally sound—free of deep settling cracks or subgrade failure—but suffers from widespread cosmetic pitting, discoloration, or rough surface wear. However, resurfacing an unstable slab is not recommended because existing cracks will quickly reflect right through the new overlay.

Comparing Upfront Costs vs. Long-Term Lifespan

While targeted repairs have a lower upfront price tag, continuing to patch a crumbling driveway year after year results in escalating maintenance expenses and diminishing visual appeal. Complete replacement requires a larger initial investment, but it resets the clock entirely. A brand-new driveway poured with proper crushed stone compaction and steel rebar reinforcement provides 30 to 40 years of maintenance-free performance, significantly elevating your home's exterior curb appeal and resale value.

Our structural evaluation techniques and repair methodologies align strictly with guidelines published by the American Concrete Institute.

Polyurethane foam jacking can temporarily level small slabs. However, if the underlying concrete is already heavily fractured or the subgrade continues to erode, lifting does not fix the broken concrete and replacement is required.

Most residential replacements take two to three working days for demolition, base compaction, forming, and pouring, followed by a 7-day curing window before passenger vehicles can drive on the surface.

Stamped Concrete vs. Pavers: Pros and Cons

When planning a major hardscape upgrade—whether a backyard entertainment patio, front walkway, or driveway—homeowners frequently find themselves debating between two premier materials: stamped concrete and interlocking pavers. Both options deliver sophisticated aesthetic appeal, rich color variations, and significant curb appeal compared to plain gray flatwork. However, they differ substantially in installation techniques, structural longevity, ongoing maintenance demands, and long-term costs. In this comprehensive comparison, Brook Concrete Company outlines the distinct pros and cons of each material to help you choose the best solution for your Dunwoody property. For detailed specifications on our decorative services, visit our stamped concrete page.

Understanding Stamped Concrete: Seamless Architectural Beauty

Stamped concrete is a continuous, poured monolithic concrete slab that is infused with integral color pigments and imprinted with specialized texturing mats while still plastic. This process creates realistic textures and grout lines mimicking natural flagstone, slate, cobblestone, or brick. Here are its primary advantages and considerations:

  • Continuous Monolithic Surface: Because stamped concrete is poured as a single reinforced slab, there are no individual sand-filled joints between stones. This means weeds, moss, and grass cannot sprout up between pattern impressions.
  • Superior Structural Stability in Clay Soils: North Georgia's expansive red clay shifts with moisture changes. Individual pavers frequently heave and sink independently, creating uneven trip ledges. Stamped concrete slabs distribute weight across a wide footprint, preventing localized settlement.
  • Faster Installation Time: Pouring and stamping an expansive backyard concrete patio typically takes only two to three days, whereas hand-laying thousands of individual pavers can require a week or more of intensive labor.
  • Lower Upfront Investment: Stamped concrete generally costs 20% to 40% less per square foot to install than high-end natural stone or interlocking pavers due to reduced manual labor.
  • Maintenance Requirements: Stamped concrete requires periodic application of a protective acrylic clear coat every two to three years to maintain color vibrancy and protect against surface abrasion.

Understanding Interlocking Pavers: Modular Versatility

Interlocking pavers consist of individual pre-cast concrete or clay brick units laid over a bedding sand layer and compacted aggregate base. Here are the main characteristics of paver systems:

  • Modular Repairability: The primary advantage of pavers is that individual damaged or stained blocks can be pulled up and replaced without tearing out the surrounding area.
  • Immediate Usability: Paver installations do not require a chemical curing period; you can walk or drive on them immediately upon completion.
  • Joint Sand Maintenance: Pavers rely on polymeric sand between joints to stay locked together. Rain and pressure washing gradually wash this sand away, requiring periodic re-sanding to prevent weed growth and shifting.
  • Susceptibility to Uneven Settling: If water erodes the sand bedding layer beneath pavers, individual blocks will sink or tilt, creating dangerous trip hazards that require manual re-leveling.

Comparing Applications: Patios, Driveways, and Pool Surrounds

Both materials perform well across diverse hardscape environments, but each has specific areas of excellence. For a custom backyard patio, stamped concrete offers unlimited artistic flexibility, allowing for sweeping organic curves and integrated seat walls. Around a concrete pool deck, stamped concrete treated with non-slip polymer additives provides a seamless, barefoot-friendly surface that prevents toe-stubbing and eliminates weed growth in wet environments.

Evaluating Long-Term Value and Return on Investment

While pavers offer modular repair benefits, their higher initial installation cost and ongoing joint maintenance requirements often make them more expensive over a ten-year horizon. Stamped concrete delivers the luxurious appearance of natural masonry at a substantially lower cost per square foot, providing an exceptional return on investment for homeowners seeking maximum aesthetic impact within budget.

Our decorative installations adhere strictly to technical standards established by the American Society of Concrete Contractors, ensuring your hardscape achieves lasting beauty and structural excellence.

Does stamped concrete crack over time?

All concrete naturally shrinks as it cures. However, by cutting control joints strategically along stamp pattern lines, any microscopic shrinkage is concealed within the grout joints, keeping the surface looking seamless.

Can stamped concrete be sealed with a slip-resistant finish?

Yes. For pool decks, steps, and walkways, we blend clear polymer anti-skid additives directly into the topcoat sealer, providing safe traction even when wet.

How Long Does Concrete Take to Cure?

Whether you have recently poured a brand-new driveway, installed a custom backyard patio, or laid a structural foundation slab, one of the most critical questions you face is: "How long does concrete take to cure?" Understanding the curing process is essential because using your new concrete surface too early can lead to permanent structural cracking, surface scarring, and reduced lifespan. In this comprehensive guide, Brook Concrete Company explains the science behind concrete curing, provides clear timelines for foot and vehicle traffic, and highlights essential protection tips for your new installation. For more on proper driveway installation, visit our concrete driveway service page.

The Critical Difference Between "Setting" and "Curing"

Many homeowners confuse concrete "setting" with concrete "curing," assuming that as soon as the surface feels hard to the touch, the job is complete. However, these two terms represent completely different physical and chemical processes:

  • Initial Setting: This is the initial hardening phase that occurs within the first 4 to 12 hours after pouring. During this window, liquid concrete stiffens into a solid mass as cement begins reacting with water, reaching a state where it can support light touch without leaving an impression.
  • Chemical Curing (Hydration): Curing is not simply "drying out." In fact, concrete does not harden by drying—it hardens through a continuous chemical reaction called hydration, in which cement particles bond with water molecules to form microscopic crystals that lock aggregate stones and sand into a rock-solid matrix. Full design compressive strength is reached at 28 days.

Standard Timelines: When Can You Walk and Drive on New Concrete?

While every pour is influenced by ambient weather conditions, here is the standard industry timeline for new concrete flatwork:

  • 24 to 48 Hours: Initial set is complete. The surface can safely handle light human foot traffic. Keep pets, bicycles, and heavy garden tools off the surface during this time to avoid scratching the tender finish.
  • 7 Days (70% Design Strength): The concrete has reached approximately 70% of its full compressive strength. It is now safe for standard passenger cars, minivans, and small SUVs to drive and park on the surface.
  • 28 Days (100% Full Design Strength): The slab has achieved its full design strength (typically 3,500 to 4,500+ PSI). It can now safely support heavy delivery trucks, RVs, dumpster roll-offs, and intensive structural framing loads on a new concrete slab.

How North Georgia Weather Influences Curing Rates

Temperature, humidity, and wind play massive roles in the hydration process. In hot, humid Dunwoody summers, surface water can evaporate too quickly before cement particles hydrate, leading to weak surface paste and hairline plastic shrinkage cracking. Our crews apply specialized liquid membrane curing compounds to trap vital moisture inside the slab. Conversely, during cold winter months, hydration slows dramatically. When temperatures dip near freezing, concrete must be protected with thermal curing blankets to prevent water from freezing inside the pores.

Common Curing Mistakes to Avoid

To ensure your new concrete achieves its maximum design strength, avoid these critical mistakes during the first month:

  • Driving on the Surface Too Early: Parking heavy vehicles before the 7-day mark puts immense tensile stress on green concrete, leading to premature cracking.
  • Applying Chemical De-Icers: Never apply salt or chemical de-icing products during the first winter season; these chemicals force moisture into concrete pores, where freeze-thaw cycles cause surface spalling.
  • Premature High-Pressure Washing: Avoid aggressive pressure washing during the first 30 days, as high-pressure water jets can erode the curing surface cream.
  • Skipping Moisture Control: In hot, sunny weather, lightly misting your new concrete with water several times a day (moist curing) significantly improves ultimate surface strength.

If unexpected surface defects or settling occur, our team provides targeted concrete repair services. Our placement and curing protocols adhere strictly to guidelines set forth by the Portland Cement Association.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does fresh concrete appear dark or blotchy while curing?

Color variations are completely normal during the first several weeks. As moisture evaporates unevenly from different depths of the slab, the concrete will gradually lighten and equalize to a uniform light gray tone.

Can I seal my new concrete immediately after pouring?

Penetrating silane/siloxane sealers or decorative acrylic topical sealers should generally not be applied until the concrete has cured for at least 28 days to prevent trapping moisture inside the slab.

How Thick Should a Residential Concrete Slab Be?

When planning any residential concrete project—whether pouring a back patio, building a detached two-car garage, erecting a storage shed, or replacing an existing driveway—one of the most critical structural decisions is determining slab thickness. Pouring a slab too thin almost guarantees premature cracking, structural settling, and costly failure under load. Conversely, over-engineering thickness adds unnecessary material expense. In this comprehensive engineering guide, Brook Concrete Company explains how to determine the optimal thickness for residential concrete slabs in Dunwoody, GA, ensuring your hardscapes provide decades of dependable performance.

Standard Thickness Recommendations by Residential Application

The intended purpose and anticipated weight load dictate the required thickness of any poured concrete slab:

  • Patios and Garden Walkways (4 Inches): Because pedestrian foot traffic, patio dining sets, and lightweight outdoor grills place minimal load on concrete, a 4-inch-thick slab (using standard 2x4 form boards) reinforced with welded wire mesh or fiber additives provides ideal structural capacity.
  • Residential Driveways and Parking Areas (4 to 5 Inches): Standard residential concrete driveways supporting passenger sedans and light SUVs are poured at a minimum of 4 inches. However, for households with heavy pickup trucks, large SUVs, or delivery traffic, upgrading to 5 inches with tied steel rebar provides vital insurance against cracking.
  • Garages, Workshops, and Heavy Equipment Pads (5 to 6 Inches): Garages and workshops support continuous heavy point loads from vehicle tires, floor jacks, toolboxes, and machinery. We recommend pouring 5 to 6 inches of 4,000 PSI concrete reinforced with a grid of #4 steel rebar.
  • Accessory Storage Sheds (4 Inches with Thickened Edges): For prefabricated backyard storage sheds, a 4-inch interior slab combined with a 10-to-12-inch thickened perimeter edge beam safely supports wall framing loads while elevating timber sill plates above ground moisture.
  • Heavy Spas, Hot Tubs, and Swim Spas (6 Inches): A filled hot tub exerts tremendous hydrostatic weight (often 4,000 to 6,000+ pounds). Poured hot tub pads should always be engineered at a minimum of 6 inches with heavy rebar reinforcement.

Why Thickness Alone Does Not Prevent Cracking

A common misconception among homeowners is that making a slab thicker will automatically solve all cracking issues. In reality, a 6-inch slab poured over poorly compacted, unlevel dirt will crack just as easily as a 4-inch slab. Slab performance is fundamentally dependent on the quality of the subgrade foundation beneath it. In northern Georgia, native red clay soils expand dramatically when wet and shrink when dry. To prevent settlement, our crews excavate unstable topsoil, install a 4-to-6-inch base of crushed granite aggregate (GAB), and mechanically compact the stone with vibrating plate tampers before pouring.

The Crucial Role of Internal Steel Reinforcement

Concrete possesses immense compressive strength (the ability to withstand crushing downward forces) but relatively low tensile strength (resistance to bending or pulling forces). When heavy vehicle wheels roll across a slab, the concrete experiences bending tension along its bottom face. We install tied steel rebar grids (typically #4 rebar on 12-to-18-inch centers) elevated on plastic chairs so the steel is positioned securely in the middle third of the slab. This internal reinforcement holds the slab together and prevents fractures from widening.

Structural Foundations vs. Floating Slabs

It is important to differentiate between floating utility slabs and load-bearing foundations. If your upcoming construction involves living spaces, home additions, or heavy masonry walls, code mandates continuous perimeter footings excavated below the local frost depth. Explore our specialized concrete foundations capabilities to learn how we engineer load-bearing footings. Our structural design standards adhere strictly to technical guidelines established by the American Concrete Institute.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if a concrete slab is poured only 3 inches thick?

A 3-inch slab lacks sufficient cross-sectional mass to withstand vehicular loads or subgrade soil movement, resulting in rapid alligator cracking and crumbling edges within months of placement.

How do you control joint spacing based on slab thickness?

Industry rule of thumb dictates that contraction joint spacing (in feet) should be no more than two to three times the slab thickness (in inches). For a 4-inch slab, control joints should be placed roughly every 8 to 10 feet.

How to Prevent Concrete Cracks

Concrete is one of the most durable, versatile, and enduring building materials on earth. However, any experienced mason will tell you an honest truth: all concrete has a natural tendency to crack. When concrete cures, it loses moisture and naturally shrinks. Furthermore, changing seasonal temperatures and expansive soil movements exert continuous stress on exterior flatwork. Fortunately, while microscopic shrinkage is normal, severe structural cracking, sunken panels, and unsightly fissures are largely preventable through proper engineering and maintenance. In this comprehensive guide, Brook Concrete Company reveals the proven construction practices and proactive homeowner maintenance steps that keep your hardscapes smooth, durable, and crack-free. For existing damage, explore our specialized concrete repair services.

1. Build on an Unyielding Subgrade Foundation

The single most important factor in crack prevention occurs before a single drop of concrete is poured. Concrete is only as stable as the soil beneath it. In north Georgia, native red clay is highly expansive, swelling during heavy rainstorms and shrinking during summer droughts. If concrete is poured directly over uncompacted soil or organic debris, rainwater will wash pockets out underneath the slab. When heavy vehicles drive over these hollow voids, the unsupported concrete snaps under the weight.

At Brook Concrete Company, we excavate all organic topsoil, install a thick 4-to-6-inch base of crushed granite aggregate (GAB), and mechanically tamp the stone using vibrating plate compactors. This dense, free-draining stone base distributes vehicle loads evenly and prevents settlement voids from forming beneath your concrete driveway.

2. Strategic Control Joint Layout and Depth

Because concrete naturally shrinks approximately 1/16 of an inch per 10 feet as moisture evaporates during hydration, stress builds within the slab. If left alone, concrete will relieve that internal tension by forming random, jagged cracks across the surface. Professional contractors manage this stress by installing control joints (contraction joints). These hand-tooled or saw-cut grooves create planned, weakened planes that guide microscopic shrinkage fractures straight down to the base where they remain completely invisible.

To be effective, control joints must be cut to a depth of at least one-quarter of the total slab thickness (1 inch deep for a 4-inch slab) and spaced at intervals no greater than 24 to 30 times the slab thickness.

3. Maintain the Proper Water-Cement Ratio

During the pouring process, adding excess water to the ready-mix truck makes the wet concrete easier and faster to rake and float. However, adding too much water drastically weakens the concrete's ultimate compressive strength. As the excess water evaporates, it leaves behind millions of microscopic voids throughout the hardened slab, dramatically increasing shrinkage and porosity. Our crews pour strict low-slump concrete mixes formulated for high strength and minimal shrinkage.

4. Implement Diligent Moist Curing Protocols

Proper curing is essential for developing maximum surface strength. If fresh concrete is exposed to high summer heat, direct sun, or dry wind, surface water evaporates too quickly, resulting in spiderweb-like plastic shrinkage cracks. We apply high-grade liquid curing compounds that form an impermeable membrane over the slab, sealing vital hydration moisture inside so the concrete develops full design strength.

5. Proactive Maintenance and Protective Sealing

Once your concrete is installed, ongoing maintenance is essential for long-term crack prevention:

  • Seal Control Joints and Cracks Immediately: Inspect your flatwork annually. Fill hairline cracks and expansion joints with commercial-grade flexible polyurethane or polyurea caulks to prevent winter water penetration.
  • Ensure Proper Surface Drainage: Keep downspout extensions directing roof runoff at least 5 to 10 feet away from slab edges to prevent sub-base soil erosion.
  • Avoid Harmful De-Icing Salts: Never apply sodium chloride or calcium chloride de-icers to exterior concrete during its first winter season; use clean sand for winter traction instead.
  • Consider Polymer Resurfacing: If surface scaling or hairline weathering begins to appear, applying an engineered overlay through concrete resurfacing can seal the surface and prevent deeper deterioration.

Our crack prevention and structural placement methodologies adhere strictly to guidelines published by the American Concrete Institute.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did my new concrete develop tiny hairline cracks?

Microscopic hairline surface crazing can occasionally occur due to rapid surface drying on hot or windy pour days. These are typically superficial cosmetic blemishes that do not compromise the structural integrity of the slab.

Can steel rebar prevent concrete from cracking?

Steel rebar does not prevent initial shrinkage cracks from forming; its purpose is to provide tensile reinforcement that holds fractured sections tightly together, preventing cracks from widening or shifting out of level.
